issues.legal_issue: Abolition of an impartible hereditary watan does not extinguish the joint family's right to partition the land when it is converted into ordinary cultivable land.
material_facts: The land had been held hereditarily as watan property, with the watan customarily held in the senior family member's name and succession governed by primogeniture.
The land was abolished as watan and converted into rayatwari land.
The High Court had dismissed the partition suit on the ground that abolition extinguished all rights, including the right to partition.
The Supreme Court relied on a Full Bench ruling and its own earlier decision disapproving that view.
issues.conclusion: Abolition did not extinguish the family's right to partition the land; the land enured for the benefit of the joint family and was partible.
issues.legal_principle: The Bombay Inferior Village Watans Abolition Act, 1958 (Bom. Act 1 of 1959), read in light of its scheme, did not extinguish the joint family's rights in the former watan land. The Court followed the Full Bench view in Laxmibai v. Ganesh and relied on Nagesh Bisto Desai and Ors. v. Khando Tirmal Desai and Ors., which disapproved the contrary view in this case and approved the Full Bench approach. The Court also rejected the contention that the distinction between the legislation considered in Nagesh Bisto Desai and the legislation concerning these watans changed the result.

issues.legal_issue: Partition of other family properties does not make unpartitioned hereditary watan land the exclusive property of the watan holder when that land continued as family property.
material_facts: Other properties capable of partition had been divided between the family branches in earlier partitions.
The watan land was not divided in those partitions and continued to pass through generations as hereditary family property, although held in the senior member's name under the custom.
The respondent argued that the earlier partitions meant no joint family remained in relation to the watan land.
issues.conclusion: The earlier partitions did not make the unpartitioned watan land the respondent's exclusive property; it continued as joint family property and was liable to partition.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the watan land as hereditary family property that had not been partitioned. The earlier division of other properties did not alter the character of this land. This conclusion accords with the Full Bench view in Laxmibai v. Ganesh and the approach approved in Nagesh Bisto Desai and Ors. v. Khando Tirmal Desai and Ors.
